terms.grammar: present subjunctive of valeō, a wish
evidence: Plaut. Truc. 2.4.79: Valeās. — Valē. (Lewis & Short s.v. valeō)

terms.grammar: valē as a quoted word, with dīcere and the dative of the person
evidence: Ov. Tr. 1.3.57: saepe ‘valē’ dictō rūrsus sum multa locūtus
Sen. Ep. 17.11: tibi valedīcere nōn licet grātīs (the compound)
terms.comment: The verb for taking leave, usually written as two words; Seneca has the compound valedīcere.

terms.grammar: jubeō with the accusative of the person and valēre
evidence: Cic. Att. 5.2.2: illum … salūtāvī, post etiam jussī valēre
terms.comment: Cicero’s phrase for greeting a man and then saying goodbye to him; compare salvēre jubeō under “greet”.

phrases.latin: «Valēte,» inquit, «bene volāte! Theodōre, patrī pārē, et aviae meīs verbīs salūtem dīc.»
phrases.english: “Goodbye,” she said, “have a good flight! Theo, do what Dad says, and give Grandma my love.”

phrases.latin: Ad portum properō. — Bene ambulātō. — Bene valētō. — Bene sit tibi.
phrases.english: I’m hurrying to the harbour. — Have a good walk. — Goodbye. — All the best.

phrases.latin: in quō illum agentem aliquid crēdō salūtāvī, post etiam jussī valēre cum mē exiēns ē suā vīllā numquid vellem rogāsset
phrases.english: there I said hello to him, busy with something, I think, and afterwards said goodbye too, when he came out of his villa and asked whether there was anything I wanted

phrases.latin: saepe ‘valē’ dictō rūrsus sum multa locūtus, et quasi discēdēns ōscula summa dedī
phrases.english: often, after saying goodbye, I went on talking at length, and gave last kisses as if I were leaving

phrases.latin: Avō et aviae valē dīc; jam abīmus.
phrases.english: Say goodbye to Grandpa and Grandma; we’re going now.

sources: Lewis & Short: valeo
